messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar, a 29-year-old Middle Eastern train conductor who had always taken pride in being composed in emergencies, came to treatment after months of feeling as though the world had turned treacherous in ways he could not switch off. The event that started it was not something that happened to him directly, but something he witnessed on a winter evening while working a late route: a man on the platform slipped near the edge, was struck and dragged badly enough that Omar saw blood soaking through the man’s coat and shining on the tracks, with torn skin and visible wounds that he could not stop looking at. He remembered the cold air on his own face and, worse, the sudden shock of the man’s skin when he tried to help, a temperature that felt unnaturally cold against his hand and seemed to lodge itself in his body long after the scene was cleared. In the days that followed, the sights and sensations from that night became potent reminders; a glimpse of blood on a customer’s knuckle, an injury on a coworker’s arm, or even the cold touch of metal on his skin could pull him back into the platform scene with a force that felt immediate and bodily, as if danger were once again right in front of him. What frightened Omar most was that these moments did not merely remind him of what had happened — they made the danger feel present, and once that sense of threat was activated he found it impossible to trust reassurance. Even when supervisors told him the line was safe or that the accident had been rare, he could not believe it for long. He began scanning every platform, every set of stairs, every person who looked unsteady, convinced that if he stopped watching something terrible would happen again.

At first he tried to push through by telling himself it was just one bad night, but sleep became a battle because he needed to stay alert. Lying in bed, he would keep the lights low and his phone near his hand, listening for noises outside his apartment and replaying the sight of blood and injuries until he was too keyed up to drift off. The next morning he would arrive at work already exhausted, yet still superalert, monitoring the crowd, the edges of the platform, the temperature of the air on his face, and anything that looked like a wound. He avoided standing too close when he passed first aid stations and found himself changing his route through the train yard if he saw an injured passenger being assisted. On colder days he covered his hands more carefully because the sharp chill on his skin could make his chest tighten with the same certainty that something was wrong. Over weeks, this constant watchfulness began to take over his days, and the more he noticed blood, injuries, or that specific cold sensation, the more convinced he became that safety was only what other people said, not something he could actually trust.

That conviction spread into his life beyond work. Omar stopped accepting late invitations from friends, and he started sitting near exits in restaurants and on trains, not because he expected a specific attack but because he felt he could never fully relax anywhere. He had been a dependable conductor, the sort of man colleagues relied on during delays and disruptions, but he began checking and rechecking even routine tasks, his attention pulled toward every possible sign of harm. The effort to stay on guard left him irritable and worn down, and he noticed that he was no longer sleeping deeply enough to recover. When a coworker brushed his forearm with a cold drink one afternoon, Omar startled sharply and had to steady himself, embarrassed by how instantly his body had reacted. That evening he could not shake the feeling that the platform had somehow followed him home, and the familiar cycle returned: the remembered scene, the body’s alarm, the refusal to believe he was safe, and the renewed need to stay watchful through the night.

By the time he sought help, it was because he feared he was becoming trapped in a life organized entirely around keeping danger at bay. He was still working, but only by forcing himself through every shift in a state of strain, and he worried that one more reminder of blood or injury would leave him unable to function at all. What he most wanted was to sleep without having to keep guard, and what he most feared was that if he let himself believe reassurance, he would miss the next catastrophe.
